prime.problem: A trained GPT-2 only returns one probability per vocabulary token for the next position. That is not text. Without a loop that picks a token and feeds it back, you can't see what the model has learned, and without a rule for which token to pick you get either the same sentence every time or nonsense from the long tail.
prime.fits: The previous card loaded OpenAI's weights and got logits of shape (B, T, 50257). This card turns those logits into text, the same multinomial draw you used for bigram names, now with a top-k cut and a model that looks at the whole prefix.
expect: why a random model gives word salad
prime.goal: Write the generation loop yourself, predict the shape at every line, and explain why top-k 50 gives varied but sensible text while a random model gives garbage.

attend: The model scores every position, so why does the loop throw away all but logits[:, -1, :]?
After multinomial you hold a number from 0 to 49. Why is that not yet a token id, and which tensor turns it into one?
How much probability does top-k 50 discard after the prompt, and what kind of tokens live in that discarded part?
With the same loop and the same seed, what exactly makes the random-init model's text meaningless?
What work does each turn of this loop repeat that it didn't need to?

must: GPT-2 predicts only the next token → text needs a loop: forward, pick one token, append, forward again → each new token is conditioned on everything written so far (autoregressive) → one bad pick changes every later step

A trained model puts most probability on a few tokens (top 50 hold 80.6% after the prompt) → the other 50,207 share the remaining 19.4% → sampling from everything draws a tail token about one step in five here → cutting to the top 50 and redrawing keeps variety but removes the tail

topk returns sorted values plus their positions → multinomial picks a slot (0–49) in the value tensor → gather maps that slot back through topk_indices to a real token id → skipping gather appends slot numbers, i.e. token ids 0–49, which decode to single characters (punctuation, digits, A–R)

Random weights → nearly flat probabilities (top 50 hold 0.54%, entropy 10.67 vs the uniform 10.83 nats) → the top-k cut removes almost nothing meaningful → the same loop writes word salad, which proves the text comes from the weights, not the loop
elevated: No KV cache: each step re-runs the model over the whole row → 8 + 9 + … + 29 = 407 positions per row instead of 29 → fine for 22 tokens, quadratic-ish waste for long generations
A seed fixes the random stream on one device only → the video's CUDA samples and your MPS samples differ with the same manual_seed(42), yet each repeats exactly on its own machine
reference: torch.multinomial accepts unnormalised weights, so no explicit division is needed
top-k 50 is the Hugging Face pipeline's default; later build-nanogpt code uses its own torch.Generator seeded 42 + ddp_rank
wrap the forward in torch.no_grad() so no graph is stored during sampling

compress.prompt: From memory, write the 8-line body of the sampling loop with the shape of every tensor as a comment, then say in two sentences why top-k 50 is there and what the random-init run proves.
checklist: forward the whole x (5, T) → logits (5, T, 50257), keep the last position (5, 50257)
softmax → probs; topk(probs, 50) → values and indices, both (5, 50)
multinomial → slot (5, 1); gather through the indices → token id (5, 1)
top-k removes the long tail (19.4% of the mass after the prompt) but keeps randomness, so 5 rows differ
random weights give flat probabilities, so the same loop writes garbage: the knowledge is in the weights

retrieve.q: Explain why generating text needs a loop around the model, when a single forward pass already produces logits at every position.
answer: each position's logits predict the token after it, given only tokens that already exist
the token after the last one doesn't exist yet, so you must pick it and feed it back
each pick changes the input for the next step, so the steps can't run in parallel

retrieve.q: Walk one row through one step: start from x of shape (5, 12) and end with x of shape (5, 13). Name every tensor and its shape.
answer: softmax → probs (5, 50257)
topk → topk_probs and topk_indices (5, 50)
multinomial → ix (5, 1), a slot 0–49
gather → xcol (5, 1), a token id

retrieve.q: You need five different continuations of a prompt for a demo, and separately one repeatable answer for a test. Which decoding rule do you pick for each, and what does each cost you?
answer: demo: top-k sampling; varied rows, but results change with the seed and device
test: greedy (k = 1); repeatable, but all rows identical and prone to loops (the measured run repeats "I'm a language model.")
sampling from all tokens gives the most variety but lets tail tokens derail the text

retrieve.q: Someone removes the gather line and appends ix directly. The code still runs. What does the output look like, and why?
answer: ix holds slots 0–49 in the sorted top-k list, not token ids
the loop then appends token ids 0–49, which are single characters in GPT-2's vocabulary: punctuation, digits and the letters A–R
shapes still match, so nothing crashes: only the text reveals the bug

compare.q: Bigram name sampling and GPT-2 sampling both call torch.multinomial in a loop. What is fundamentally different about the probabilities they draw from, and which design choice causes it?
answer: bigram: one row of a 27 × 27 table, chosen by the last character only
GPT-2: a fresh 50,257-way distribution computed from the whole prefix by 12 blocks of attention
cause: the bigram model's context is one character; GPT-2's is up to 1024 tokens
with 27 options there's no tail to cut, so the bigram loop needs no top-k; with 50,257 tokens the tail matters

compare.q: The Shakespeare GPT's generate sampled from all 65 characters with no top-k. Why was that acceptable there, and what would go wrong if you used the same rule on GPT-2?
answer: 65 characters: each is a plausible option, and the tail is small
50,257 tokens: 19.4% of the mass sits on 50,207 unlikely tokens after this prompt
without top-k, GPT-2 draws a tail token about one step in five here and can derail
same loop shape in both: forward, last position, softmax, draw, append

predict.q: Over the lab's 22 steps × 5 rows, the top-50 mass averaged 0.79 but dropped to 0.1613 at one step. At that step, what does top-k do to the other 84% of the probability, and would top-p 0.9 keep more or fewer than 50 tokens there?
predict.answer: Top-k sets that 84% to zero and scales the kept 16% up to 100%, so each kept token's chance grows about 6× (1 / 0.1613 = 6.2). The model was very unsure there, so many plausible tokens were dropped. Top-p 0.9 would keep far more than 50 tokens, since 50 tokens cover only 16%: that step is exactly where a fixed k and an adaptive p disagree most.
